summary: Defines GS2, a family of SASL mechanisms that lets any suitable GSS-API mechanism be used for authentication in SASL. It improves on the older SASL GSSAPI mechanism, can use fewer messages, and supports negotiable channel binding. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: One standard doorway lets many kinds of ID cards work, and the doorway can check you are in the right room too.

questions: what does the plus suffix mean in sasl mechanism names
subtitle: A bridge that lets any suitable GSS-API security mechanism be used as a SASL login method, with optional channel binding.

tldr.problem: The older SASL bridge to GSS-API (called GS1 here) was not round-trip optimized and did not support channel binding, and it never caught on for any mechanism other than Kerberos V5.
tldr.mechanism: GS2 wraps the GSS-API security context tokens in SASL messages and adds only a small header to the first token. That header carries a channel binding flag and an optional authorization identity.
tldr.outcome: Any GSS-API mechanism that supports mutual authentication and channel binding gets two SASL names, one plain and one with the -PLUS suffix. GS2 has no security layers, so the RFC strongly recommends channel binding to a secure channel such as TLS.

facts.label: Name hash
facts.value: First 55 bits of the SHA-1 hash of the OID's DER encoding, Base32 encoded

today: RFC 5801 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9266. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why GS2 Exists
sections.content:
GSS-API is a framework that gives applications security services through many authentication mechanisms. SASL is a framework that adds authentication and security layers to connection-based protocols, also through many mechanisms. RFC 5801 describes how to use a GSS-API mechanism as though it were a SASL mechanism. The facility is called GS2, a moniker meaning the second GSS-API to SASL bridge. The first, which the RFC calls GS1, came from RFC 2222 and is now RFC 4752.

GS1 failed to gain wide deployment for any GSS-API mechanism other than Kerberos V5. It was not round-trip optimized and it did not support channel binding. Those problems, plus the chance to offer the SCRAM password mechanism through GSS-API, motivated GS2.

GS2 is meant to be as simple as possible. It adds a small header (a few bytes plus the length of the client-requested authorization identity) to the initial GSS-API context token. It does not protect plaintext outside GS2, such as SASL mechanism negotiation, unless channel binding to a secure channel is used.
sections.eli5: The first doorway only worked well for one kind of ID card and made you walk back and forth too often. GS2 is a new doorway that is simpler and works with many more cards.

sections.title: Mechanism Names
sections.content:
Every GSS-API mechanism used through GS2 has two SASL mechanism names. The plain name means the server does not support channel binding. Adding the suffix -PLUS gives the name that means the server does support it.

If the mechanism's own specification gave it a SASL name, that name is used. Otherwise the name is GS2- followed by the Base32 encoding (uppercase alphabet) of the first 55 bits of the SHA-1 hash of the DER encoding of the mechanism's Object Identifier. The RFC works this out by hand for SPKM-1, giving GS2-DT4PIK22T6A.

Kerberos V5 is a special case. Its OID would give GS2-QLJHGJLWNPL, but the RFC assigns the shorter names GS2-KRB5 and GS2-KRB5-PLUS instead. Sections 10 and 11 also define two GSS-API calls, GSS_Inquire_SASLname_for_mech and GSS_Inquire_mech_for_SASLname, so that implementations can map between mechanisms and SASL names. If neither a lookup nor another mapping works, the implementation MUST NOT use that mechanism.
sections.eli5: Each kind of ID card gets two name tags: a plain one, and one with PLUS on it for doorways that also check the room. If a card has no name tag yet, the name is made by scrambling its serial number.

sections.title: The GS2 Header and Message Flow
sections.content:
The SASL client always acts as the GSS-API initiator and the server as the acceptor. After the first message, every SASL message is exactly the same as the GSS-API security context token. The first token is changed in two ways. The standard token header from RFC 2743 MUST be removed if present, and a GS2 header MUST be put in front of the result.

The header has the form [gs2-nonstd-flag ","] gs2-cb-flag "," [gs2-authzid] ",". The optional F flag says the standard token header was missing, so the server must not restore it. The channel binding flag is p= plus a binding type name, or n, or y. The optional authorization identity is written a= followed by a name, in UTF-8 with commas sent as =2C and equals signs as =3D.

GS2 does not use any GSS-API per-message tokens. The mutual authentication request flag MUST be set, and the client MUST check that the matching returned flag is set once the context is established, or authentication MUST fail.
sections.eli5: The first message gets a little sticky note on the front. The note says whether the sender can check the room, and optionally who they want to be treated as.

sections.title: Negotiating Channel Binding
sections.content:
Channel binding ties the authentication to an outer secure channel such as TLS. Because GS2 has no security layers, the negotiation of channel binding itself must be integrity protected, and GS2 does this by including the GS2 header in the channel binding data.

Servers that support channel binding SHOULD advertise both the plain and PLUS names of each mechanism. A server that would never accept the plain variant for policy reasons MUST advertise only the PLUS variant. A client that supports negotiation and sees the PLUS name MUST use p. A client that does not support channel binding MUST use n. A client that supports it but did not see the PLUS name uses y.

The server fails authentication if the client sent y and the server did advertise the PLUS variant, which would indicate that something removed the PLUS name along the way. It also fails if the client sent p for a binding type the server does not support, or sent n while the server requires channel binding.

The default channel binding type is tls-unique. Servers MUST implement it if they implement any channel binding, and clients SHOULD.
sections.eli5: The flag is a way of saying whether you checked you are in the right room. If you say you could not check, but the doorway knows it offers room checking, someone probably tampered with the sign, so the door stays shut.

sections.title: Example Exchanges
sections.content:
The RFC gives seven examples. In every one, the server starts with an empty challenge, because GSS-API authentication is always started by the client and SASL lets either side go first.

Example 1 is a one round-trip exchange with no channel binding and an authorization identity of someuser. Example 3 shows a client that sends the F flag because its first token had no standard header. Examples 4 to 6 use channel binding with tls-unique or tls-server-end-point, the latter noted as needing out-of-band negotiation. Example 7 shows a client that supports channel binding but sees a server that does not, so it sends y.

The number of messages on success equals the number of context tokens the GSS-API mechanism would normally need to establish a security context.
sections.eli5: Every conversation starts the same way: the doorkeeper says nothing, you show your card with the sticky note, and the two of you pass notes back and forth until the doorkeeper says yes or no.

sections.title: Coexisting with GSSAPI and SPNEGO
sections.content:
Kerberos V5 can be used in SASL under the old name GSSAPI and also through GS2, but the two are not wire compatible. A server that supports Kerberos V5 under GS2 SHOULD also support it through GSSAPI to work with older clients. If an application needs SASL security layers, it MUST use GSSAPI instead of GS2-KRB5. If it can use channel binding to an external channel, selecting Kerberos V5 through GS2 is RECOMMENDED.

GSS-API mechanisms that themselves negotiate other mechanisms, such as SPNEGO, MUST NOT be used with GS2. They interact badly with SASL mechanism negotiation: negotiation can fail, and a client could end up on a less preferred mechanism. The RFC assigns the names SPNEGO and SPNEGO-PLUS only to help library writers, and SASL clients MUST NOT choose them.
sections.eli5: The old doorway and the new doorway speak slightly different languages, so a building should keep both open for a while. And a card that secretly picks another card for you is banned, because it could pick a worse one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of a GS2 mechanism depends on the underlying GSS-API mechanism. GSS-API mechanisms that do not support channel binding cannot be used through GS2. Because there are no security layers, the RFC says it is strongly RECOMMENDED to use channel binding to a secure external channel. Successful channel binding eliminates man-in-the-middle attacks, provided that the channel, its binding data and the GSS-API mechanism are secure.

Channel binding also protects the SASL mechanism negotiation, since an untampered secure channel protected it. Clients SHOULD NOT canonicalize the server's host name using an insecure directory service such as DNS without DNSSEC. SHA-1 is used only to derive names, so no traditional cryptographic properties are needed from it.

GS2 does not protect against downgrade attacks on the channel binding type. Negotiating the type was intentionally left out of scope.
sections.eli5: The doorway is only as strong as the ID card behind it, and it cannot hide what you say after you are inside. Use a locked tunnel to the door as well, and be careful that nobody tricks you about which door you are at.

data.title: GS2 header
data.code:
gs2-authzid     = "a=" saslname
gs2-nonstd-flag = "F"
gs2-cb-flag     = ("p=" cb-name) / "n" / "y"
gs2-header      = [gs2-nonstd-flag ","] gs2-cb-flag ","
                  [gs2-authzid] ","
